title: SSL/TLS Certificate Management on RHEL 9 with NGINX
description: Learn HTTPS from the beginning, issue certificates with a private practice CA, renew safely and troubleshoot the user-facing result.
baseline: RHEL 9 · NGINX · OpenSSL 3 · two isolated VMware VMs · app.example.mil is a fictional private lab name
prerequisite: Start with Before You Start. We will create the two small private servers and explain each tool before using it. You need no previous Linux administration experience.
supplies: A Windows host and two new private RHEL 9 VMs, or follow our first lesson to build them.
A valid RHEL entitlement, trusted RHEL ISO, VMware Workstation Pro and a current Firefox for a disposable practice profile.
Enough spare memory for two 2 GB VMs and host space for two growable 30 GB disks plus updates. No cloud resources or real DoD account are needed.

steps.title: Write down the two jobs
steps.where: Your Windows host · Notepad lab notes
actions: On your Windows PC, click Start, type Notepad, and open it. Save a new file as TLS lab notes.txt in Documents.
Write: application server (TLS-APP01) = NGINX plus our small hosted practice page, 10.90.0.10/24.
Write: practice CA server (TLS-CA01) = a pretend signing office, 10.90.0.20/24. It is not a DoD CA.
Write: app.example.mil = the browser address for the practice application. It is a fictional example used only by private hosts-file entries in this lab, not a domain you own.
Write: learner = the Linux user we will create on both new VMs. Keep passwords in your password manager, not this notes file.

This course builds the TLS layer, not an enterprise firewall. The architecture diagram shows a real edge-firewall pattern; our host-only network and RHEL firewalld model a private practice boundary. Never publish these VMs.

steps.title: Create the private practice network
steps.where: Your Windows 10 host · VMware Workstation Pro 17
actions: At each Linux console, run the shutdown command below. Wait until both VMs show Powered off.
In VMware, choose Edit, then Virtual Network Editor. Click Change Settings and accept the Windows administrator prompt.

steps.title: Give the application server its private address
steps.where: TLS-APP01 · RHEL 9 local console · Bash

steps.title: Open PowerShell and verify SSH host keys
steps.where: Your Windows 10 host · Windows PowerShell
actions: On Windows, click Start, type PowerShell, and open Windows PowerShell as your normal user.
Run Get-Command ssh. If SSH is missing, open PowerShell as administrator and run Add-WindowsCapability -Online -Name OpenSSH.Client~~~~0.0.1.0, then reopen normal PowerShell.

Back in normal PowerShell, run ssh learner@10.90.0.10. Compare the displayed fingerprint with the application console before typing yes. Enter your learner password when asked.
Run hostname in the SSH session. Type exit to return to Windows. Repeat ssh learner@10.90.0.20 and compare the CA fingerprint, then run hostname and exit.

actions: Open the interactive architecture below. Select External users, then Firewall, then the RHEL application server, then NGINX, then Hosted application.

steps.title: Understand TLS and HTTPS
steps.where: Your Windows host · Notepad lab notes
actions: Think of HTTPS as a protected delivery envelope for HTTP messages.
TLS encrypts traffic in transit, checks that messages were not changed, and helps the client authenticate the endpoint when it validates the certificate.
SSL is the older protocol family; people still say SSL certificate, but this lab uses TLS 1.2 and TLS 1.3, not SSL, TLS 1.0 or TLS 1.1.
HTTPS does not prove an application has no bugs or that every person using it is authorized.

guide.why: Using an old name must not lead us to enable obsolete protocols.

guide.failure: If you confuse an application login password with TLS, reread the envelope analogy: they solve different problems.

steps.title: Meet the public certificate and secret key
steps.where: Your Windows host · Notepad lab notes
actions: Think of a certificate as a school ID card showing a name, an issuer and an expiry date. The real certificate also contains a public key.
Think of the private key as the secret way the server proves it owns that public key. It is not copied into the certificate.

steps.title: Build the trust chain
steps.where: Your Windows host · Notepad lab notes
actions: The website leaf certificate is like your ID. An intermediate CA is the office allowed to issue it. A root CA is the top trust anchor.
The root signs the intermediate; the intermediate signs the website certificate. The root private key is especially sensitive and normally kept offline in a real PKI.
NGINX sends the website certificate first, then the intermediate certificates in order. It normally does not send the root.
The client separately decides which roots to trust. Receiving a root from a random website does not make it trusted.
